title: Into the forest
hookLine: a second game, a stake of forest and hiding, and the people of the city follow the Pandavas out
carry: vanaprastha: the forest is for growing, not only loss
tomorrow: How do you feed guests with nothing?

lines: CALLED BACK FOR ONE MORE GAME.
THE BOOK OF THE FOREST BEGINS.
cards: The Pandavas set out for home, free, with their weapons and their chariots. They don't get far. Back in the hall, Duryodhana is already talking to his father.
In the telling, a messenger catches up with Yudhishthira on the road and calls him back for one more game. The stake this time isn't gold or brothers. It's exile.
The book of the hall closes, and the long book of the forest, the Vana, begins.

teach.b: Yudhishthira hears the summons, and turns around. Good and evil come to beings as the creator ordains, he says, and summoned by the old king, he won't refuse.

The terms: whoever loses goes into the forest for twelve years, in deer skins, then spends a thirteenth year in some town without being recognized. If they're found in that year, it begins again. Shakuni throws, and wins.
As the Pandavas leave, Vidura describes each of them to the blind king. Yudhishthira covers his face. Bhima looks at his great arms.
Arjuna scatters sand as he walks. The twins smear themselves with dust. Draupadi goes weeping, her face hidden by her loosened hair.
Kunti stays behind in Vidura's house.
Then, as the Vana Parva opens, the people of the city follow them out, and Yudhishthira has to ask them, gently, to go home. Vana means forest. For the Pandavas it's loss.

But in Hindu teaching the forest is never only loss. It's where the rishis lived and taught; some of the old Vedic texts are called the Aranyakas, the forest books. And a stage of life is named for it.

Hindu tradition describes four stages, the ashramas: student, householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller, when a person steps back from running the house and turns toward God, and last, sannyasa, letting go of everything.

Few people move to a real forest now. But many Hindu grandparents still speak of their vanaprastha years: giving things away, more prayer, more temple, pilgrimage. The Pandavas didn't choose their forest.
It will still be where they hear more teaching than anywhere else.

how: The Vana Parva, the book of the forest, is read and retold for the many stories the Pandavas hear in exile; and the forest names a stage of Hindu life, vanaprastha, that many elders still speak of.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira, free and on the road home. a messenger says the old king calls you back for one more game. what do you do?
games.why: he goes back, saying good and evil come as the creator ordains, and loses: twelve years in the forest and a year in hiding.

practice: Choose one thing you own and don't need, a book, a shirt, something kept out of habit, and decide who could use it. Many Hindu elders begin their vanaprastha years just like this, with dana, giving.
If you pray, offer the giving to God; if you don't, notice what it feels like to set one thing down.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest, where the Pandavas go after the second game, in deer skins, with the people of their city following them out.

orig.note: Sanskrit vana: forest; the Vana Parva is the book of the forest.

carryVoice: Your line: vanaprastha: the forest is for growing, not only loss. The city walked out with them. Until tomorrow.
